node.name: Sunday Trivia Nights at Bobbi’s
node.descriptionText:
Trivia at Bobbi’s runs about 90 minutes and is played over five rounds. The game features a slideshow format with image-based and puzzle categories, making it engaging, easy to follow, and accessible for players with hearing difficulties.

Questions span history, science, music, film, television, geography, and more, creating a well-rounded game that appeals to players of all experience levels and interests.

A strong emphasis is placed on teamwork, with categories designed to encourage group thinking and collaboration. Bobbi’s puzzle rounds are especially popular, known for their creativity and memorable “A-ha!” moments.

Trivia at Bobbi’s is always free to play, with prizes and bragging rights for the top-scoring teams. All are welcome!

node.name: Volunteer with Sunrise Cafe!
node.descriptionText:
Start your morning off on a great note! Join Dwight Hall Monday and Wednesday mornings to volunteer at Sunrise Cafe. Sunrise Cafe is an early morning soup kitchen that serves New Haven's homeless and food-insecure every weekday from 6:30 A.M. to 8:30 A.M. The service site is located at 57 Olive St., just a 15 minute walk from Phelps Gate. Volunteers will meet in front of Phelps Gate at 6:00am, walk together to Sunrise Cafe, and will return to campus by 9:00am.

To sign up, please request to join DWIGHT HALL VOLUNTEER CORPS, and we will approve your request as soon as possible.

Sunrise Cafe has been serving breakfast without charge to New Haven's homeless and hungry since 2015. Each weekday morning, the Cafe welcomes guests to the undercroft of St. Paul and St. James, near Wooster Square and three blocks south of the New Haven Green with white tablecloths, flowers and a rotating menu of fresh, warm, nutritious home-cooked food. Your generosity opens our doors.

Cheerful volunteers take each order individually, deliver the breakfast to our guest and help our paid chefs in the kitchen. Staff and volunteers ensure every guest is warmly welcomed.

Sunrise Cafe is uniquely welcoming and secure, based on trust and mutual respect, and the rapport built between the volunteer servers and our guests. With a warm welcome and just two rules – no drugs on the premises and no arguments – Sunrise has become a community center for the homeless, a place to come every weekday morning and gather with friends.

Hungry friends come for the home-cooked, nourishing breakfast and stay for simple medical services offered by the Cornell Scott Health Center and access to support from social services to find housing.

Sunrise provides a unique opportunity to bridge New Haven's inequalities that separate us from one another. Volunteers come once and become regulars. Guests and volunteers become friends and greet one another on the street.

If you have any questions, email maryann.dang@yale.edu

node.name: Graphite from Waste? Rethinking Supply Chains for a Critical Battery Material
node.descriptionText:
Nearly every lithium-ion battery depends on graphite, yet global supply is highly concentrated and carries a heavy environmental footprint. As battery demand grows, a pressing question for industrial ecologists is whether carbon-rich waste streams, such as biomass residues and waste plastics, can become a meaningful, lower-impact source of this critical material.

This session, which is part of International Industrial Ecology Day 2026, invites researchers, practitioners, and policymakers interested in critical materials, the circular economy, and clean-energy supply chains to explore that question from several angles. How much waste feedstock is available, and where? Which conversion technologies are emerging? How do they compare in terms of life-cycle environmental and economic performance? And which policies, including environmental justice considerations, will decide where waste-derived graphite facilities are located, and who benefits? Short talks drawing on material flow analysis, life cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, and policy analysis will set the stage for an open discussion.

Join the conversation: What would it take to move waste-derived graphite from lab to market? What lessons carry over from other critical materials? We especially welcome perspectives from different regions, industries, and material systems.
The 60-minute session opens with a 5-minute welcome and framing, followed by four 10-minute talks and a 15-minute open discussion:
1. Waste-to-Graphite: Where Are the Opportunities, and What Stands in the Way? Bingquan Zhang
2. Can Graphite from Biomass Compete on Cost and Environmental Impacts in the U.S.? Hannah Wang
3. How Much Could Waste PET Plastics Contribute to the Future Graphite Supply in the U.S.? Barbara Reck
4. What Policies Will Shape the Siting of Waste-Derived Graphite Facilities in the U.S.? Robert Klee
Open Discussion (15 min)
The session closes with an open conversation among speakers and participants. Questions, comments, and experiences from all attendees are warmly welcome.
Speakers
All speakers are from the Yale School of the Environment, Yale University.
Dr. Yuan Yao (moderator), Professor; Director, Center for Industrial Ecology
Dr. Bingquan Zhang, Postdoctoral Associate, Center for Industrial Ecology
Ms. Hannah Wang, Ph.D. Student, Center for Industrial Ecology
Dr. Barbara Reck, Senior Research Scientist, Center for Industrial Ecology
Dr. Robert Klee, Senior Associate Dean for P

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Beyond Prediction: Toward Trustworthy and Human-Centered GeoAI
node.descriptionText:
Dear colleagues,

Please join us for a presentation by Zhe Zhang, Associate Professor of Geography at Texas A&M University:

Beyond Prediction: Toward Trustworthy and Human-Centered GeoAI

Monday, November 30
12:00–1:00 p.m.
Digital Humanities Lab
• Building: Sterling Memorial Library (First Floor)
• Street Address: 120 High St, New Haven, CT 06511

Lunch will be provided.

Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) has expanded our capacity to model complex spatial and spatiotemporal processes, but critical challenges remain around uncertainty, explainability, heterogeneous data integration, and meaningful human decision-making. In this talk, Professor Zhang will explore advances in trustworthy, human-centered GeoAI across three connected areas: 
(1) uncertainty-aware GeoAI for transportation and infrastructure systems;  
(2) multimodal GeoAI for disaster and infrastructure resilience; and  
(3) spatiotemporal modeling and explainable AI that helps decision-makers understand the geographic, temporal, and contextual factors behind model outcomes.


Professor Zhang’s work brings computational intelligence together with geographic context, domain expertise, and human knowledge to advance more transparent, collaborative, and context-aware spatial decision-support systems.


About the speaker:
Zhe Zhang is an Associate Professor in the Department of Geography at Texas A&M University, with joint appointments in Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Texas A&M Hazard Reduction and Recovery Center. Her research focuses on participatory GIS, spatial decision support, human–AI interaction, and trustworthy GeoAI. Her work has been supported by the NSF, NASA, USDOT, NOAA, and the National Geographic Society. She is the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, the Distinguished Contributions Award from Women in GIS, and the 2022–2024 ISPRS Jack Dangermond Best Paper Award.


We hope you can join us.

node.name: Monday Mindfulness Meditation
node.descriptionText:
Free afternoon group meditation held on Zoom sponsored by Being Well at Yale (Employee Well-being).  Sessions are held during the academic year September through mid-December and mid-January through end of May. 

Taking a break during the workday to pause and practice mindfulness has been shown to be beneficial for enhancing executive function, increasing emotional regulation, and reducing cortisol levels. Meditations are a mix of guided and silent. Time for reflections and optional sharing is also included at the conclusion of the practice. 

Beginners welcome! No experience necessary. No special equipment required. Open to Yale University employees. 

Sessions are led by Danielle Casioppo, Education Specialist and Certified Mindfulness-Based Strengths Practice instructor with Being Well at Yale / Employee Well-being. 

To join please send a request to beingwell@yale.edu and specify your Yale affiliation. You will then be added to the Yale meditation email list serve. The Zoom link to join the sessions is included in the weekly reminder emails.

node.name: [RESCHEDULED for 11/30] ITW: Collective Knowledge
node.descriptionText: Where do you know from? The goal of the workshop is to reframe our understanding of how knowledge is produced and shared in the classroom to consider ‘knowing’ a collective practice. The workshop will utilize pedagogical scholarship to help participants expand their teaching practice beyond traditional models of knowledge transfer. We will begin with a group reflection of our respective disciplinary models of knowing and learning and personal teaching praxis. Following, as a group we will develop a shared definition of collective knowledge and teaching that leaves room for how this concept may be implemented in one’s own classroom, discussion section or lab. We will then workshop strategies for incorporating students’ lived experiences into the classroom with the goal of supporting students as they become co-creators of knowledge. Please contact the facilitators, Molly Blondell (molly.blondell@yale.edu) and Ulas Berk Karli (ulasberk.karli@yale.edu) with any questions.

node.descriptionText: Join course instructor Jake Halpern and student alumni to learn more about this creative writing course in Stockholm, Sweden!
node.descriptionHtml:
Join course instructor Jake Halpern and student alumni to learn more about this creative writing course in Stockholm, Sweden!

Over this four-week extended writer's retreat, you can finally start that young adult novel you've always been meaning to write. You'll celebrate Midsummer on a remote island deep in the Stockholm archipelago, hold writing sessions on ancient Viking burial mounds and explore abandoned Viking settlements. You'll also swim in pristine Swedish lakes, have outdoor barbecues, and sweat it out in traditional Scandinavian saunas.
